Devon
DEV-un
n. (the large south-western English county of Exeter and the Channel ports, which withstood the 1549 rebels and burned Agnes Prest in 1557)
Old English Defnas, from the British tribal name Dumnonii; the shire name is Defenascir.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Devon is the great county between Cornwall and Somerset, holding the cathedral city of Exeter, the Channel ports of Plymouth and Dartmouth and the north-coast harbours. Its Reformation history turns on two events. In 1549 the western rebels, chiefly Cornish but joined by men of east Devon, besieged Exeter for five weeks; the city held for the crown and the new service, and the siege was raised in August. Eight years later, under Mary, Agnes Prest, a poor woman of Boyton, was tried for denying that Christ's natural body was in the sacrament and burned outside Exeter in 1557; Foxe records her examination, in which she answered the bishop's chaplains out of the Scriptures and was reckoned mad because she would not retract. Devon men went out to sea in great numbers under Elizabeth, and Plymouth was the port from which the Leiden congregation sailed in 1620. The county's dissent was strong after the Great Ejection, and Exeter's own assembly was the scene of the Arian controversy of 1719 that split the western Presbyterians. The dictionary records the martyr before the admirals and holds that a poor woman's confession at a stake is the county's chief ornament.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who suffers death for his religion; a stake as a post set in the ground; recantation as the retracting of a declaration; a confession as an acknowledgment; and a siege as the surrounding of a place by an army.

expand to see more

MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defence of the Christian faith, or in defence of any cause which he believes to be true.

STAKE, n. A small piece of wood sharpened and set in the ground; the post to which one condemned to be burnt was fastened.

RECANTATION, n. The act of recanting; a retraction of a former declaration or opinion.

CONFESSION, n. Acknowledgment; the acknowledgment of a crime or fault; a profession of belief.

SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place, for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.

Key Scripture

Rev 6:9 — "And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:"

Heb 11:37 — "They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;"

Mat 5:10 — "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

Rev 12:11 — "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death."

Modern Corruption

South-western county whose city of Exeter held against the western rebels in 1549 and outside whose walls Agnes Prest was burned in 1557 for denying the corporal presence in the sacrament.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the doctrine for which Agnes Prest was killed, the claim that the natural body of Christ is corporally present under the species of bread, and the dictionary names it by its name, transubstantiation, defined at the Fourth Lateran Council and enforced in England by burning. A poor and unlettered woman of Boyton saw through it on the plain ground that a body cannot be in heaven and in ten thousand places at once, and she died for the seeing. John's vision assigns her her place: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9). The dictionary does not call her death a tragic consequence of religious division; it calls it a murder done for a false doctrine.

The second paragraph is against a modern softening that is kinder to the persecutor than to the martyr, treating the Marian burnings as an excess of an age rather than the enforcement of a teaching. Scripture gives the sufferers a catalogue and a verdict: “They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword” (Heb 11:37), and the Lord Himself pronounces, “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10). The victory is located where Prest located it, in the blood of another and in a testimony held to the end, for “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11). Devon sent out famous seamen; it sent up one better witness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek psuche (G5590), a soul or life; Greek marturia (G3141), a testimony; Greek dioko (G1377), to persecute.

expand to see more

Greek psuche (G5590) — the soul, the life; “the souls of them that were slain”, Revelation 6:9.

Greek marturia (G3141) — a testimony, a witness borne; “the testimony which they held”, Revelation 6:9.

Greek prizo (G4249) — to saw asunder; “they were sawn asunder”, Hebrews 11:37.

Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, to persecute; “Blessed are they which are persecuted”, Matthew 5:10.

Greek nikao (G3528) — to conquer, to overcome; “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb”, Revelation 12:11.

Usage

"“the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) — Agnes Prest burned outside Exeter, 1557."

"“Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness” (Mat 5:10) — her examination recorded by Foxe."

"“they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — a refusal to retract reckoned madness."
